cut.ch1_intro.title: April 1661 · Lakjemuyse
cut.ch1_intro.1: Koxinga's fleet sailed from Liaoluo Bay on Kinmen, waited for favorable winds at Penghu, then crossed the strait eastward.
cut.ch1_intro.2: He Bin, a former interpreter for the Dutch East India Company, presented a map marking the Lakjemuyse channel: a shallow passage the Dutch thought impassable for large ships, which junks could cross at high tide.
cut.ch1_intro.3: Tayouan's garrison numbered about nine hundred. Both sides knew the coming days would decide who held the Taijiang inner sea.
cut.ch2_intro.title: May 1661 · Saccam
cut.ch2_intro.1: After the Zheng landing, Fort Provintia at Saccam was cut off. Its commander, Valentyn, had only a hundred-odd soldiers.
cut.ch2_intro.2: Fort Zeelandia across the water could not help. The Han farmers around Saccam, and villages such as Sinkan, waited to see which way things would go.
cut.ch2_hambroek.title: Call to Surrender
cut.ch2_hambroek.1: The Zheng army sent the captured minister Hambroek into Fort Zeelandia to urge surrender. Coyett refused.
cut.ch2_hambroek.2: Hambroek was killed after returning to the Zheng camp. During the siege, both sides are recorded as having killed prisoners.
cut.ch2_siege.title: Turning to Siege
cut.ch2_siege.1: The bastions' crossfire made a frontal assault ruinously costly.
cut.ch2_siege.2: The Zheng army instead built camps and tuntian (military farms) outside the walls, preparing for a long siege.
cut.ch3_intro.title: Summer 1661 · Relief
cut.ch3_intro.1: When word reached Batavia, it sent Jacob Caeuw with about twelve ships and seven hundred men to the rescue.
cut.ch3_intro.2: The Zheng army set up batteries on Baxemboy and along the Tayouan shore, waiting for the fleet to enter the inner sea.
cut.ch4_intro.title: December 1661 · Redoubt Utrecht
cut.ch4_intro.1: Caeuw left Taiwan with his ships, claiming to seek contact with the Qing court, but actually returned to Batavia. Morale in the fort hit bottom, and grain and powder ran ever shorter.
cut.ch4_intro.2: On the high ground beside Fort Zeelandia, Redoubt Utrecht overlooks the fort. Whoever holds the redoubt holds the fort's lifeline.
cut.ch4_treaty.title: 1 February 1662 · The Treaty
cut.ch4_treaty.1: Coyett signed an eighteen-article treaty with Koxinga and surrendered Fort Zeelandia.
cut.ch4_treaty.2: The Dutch were allowed to leave with their personal belongings and supplies for the voyage, ending thirty-eight years of Dutch rule in Taiwan.
cut.ch4_treaty.3: Over nine months of siege, both sides paid heavily: about half of the Zheng forces in Taiwan died of disease, in battle, or in indigenous attacks.
menu.subtitle: Siege of Fort Zeelandia · 1661–1662
ending.zheng_swift.title: Swift War
ending.zheng_swift: The Zheng army succeeded at every turn, and Fort Zeelandia had no room left to resist before relief arrived. Speed meant less disease and fewer casualties, but the cost of war did not vanish: the soldiers, Han farmers and villages caught up in it all lost family or homes in these few months.
ending.historical.title: Nine-Month Siege
ending.historical: As in history, Fort Zeelandia negotiated its surrender after a long siege. Thirty-eight years of Dutch rule in Taiwan ended, and the Zheng established a regime along the Taijiang shore. Victory went to the Zheng, but both sides paid heavily.
ending.zheng_costly.title: Pyrrhic Victory
ending.zheng_costly: Fort Zeelandia changed hands in the end, but a string of setbacks left the Zheng army badly weakened. Disease, casualties and indigenous counterattacks made this victory heavier than in history.
ending.voc_holds.title: The Fort Stands
ending.voc_holds: Redoubt Utrecht held, and Fort Zeelandia survived the winter. This did not happen in history: in this version the Company's flag still flies over Tayouan, and both sides of the siege must still face the disease and famine of the next season.
ending.voc_relieved.title: Relief Arrives
ending.voc_relieved: The relief force from Batavia landed, and the garrison regained its footing. The Zheng army fell back toward Saccam. Control of the Taijiang inner sea remains unresolved, and the Han farmers and villages caught between the two sides must still survive between two armed regimes.
ending.koxinga_falls.title: The Commander Falls
ending.koxinga_falls: Koxinga died in the fighting, and the expedition lost its commander. In history, he died of illness in June 1662, months after taking Fort Zeelandia; in this version, the campaign ended abruptly in his hands.
history.ch1: Chapter 1 · History: On 30 April 1661, the Zheng army passed through Lakjemuyse at high tide into the Taijiang inner sea. On 1 May, Thomas Pedel led about 240 musketeers in a sortie onto Baxemboy and was routed; he and 118 men were killed. The same day the main Dutch warship, the Hector, exploded and sank.
history.ch2: Chapter 2 · History: Fort Provintia, cut off for several days, surrendered on 4 May. The Zheng army sent Hambroek to urge Fort Zeelandia to surrender without success; a frontal assault on the fort failed, and it turned to a long siege. Sinkan and other villages accepted Zheng overtures.
history.ch3: Chapter 3 · History: Jacob Caeuw arrived with the relief force. On 16 September a combined sea and land counterattack failed; the flagship Koukercken ran aground and sank, with the loss of several small boats and about 130 men.
history.ch4: Chapter 4 · History: After the relief fleet left, the garrison's morale collapsed. On 25 January 1662 the Zheng army took Redoubt Utrecht (according to Dutch records, using intelligence from the deserter Radis; Chinese sources do not mention this). On 1 February Coyett signed the treaty and surrendered Fort Zeelandia.

codex.laborer.title: Laborer
codex.laborer.intro: Zheng army labor corps: hauling, logging, building camps and digging.
codex.laborer.history: Many of the expedition's 20,000-plus people were non-combatants; the camps, military farms and siege works after the landing all depended on them.
codex.laborer.design: Can gather, build and dig tunnels, but fights very poorly; their numbers set the pace of your works.
codex.shield_soldier.title: Rattan Shield Soldier
codex.shield_soldier.intro: Infantry with rattan shields and short swords.
codex.shield_soldier.history: Light and resilient, rattan shields were common gear in late-Ming Fujian and Guangdong armies, used against arrows, blades and spears.
codex.shield_soldier.design: 30% chance to fully block arrows; cost-effective, but still vulnerable to muskets and artillery.
codex.archer_zheng.title: Archer
codex.archer_zheng.history: Dutch records of the battle on Baxemboy say Zheng arrow volleys shook the Dutch musketeers' formation.
codex.archer_zheng.design: Shorter range and lower damage than VOC musketeers, but cheap and uses no powder.
codex.iron_man.title: Iron Men
codex.iron_man.intro: Elite heavily armored infantry with long blades (the Dutch called them "iron men").
codex.iron_man.history: Koxinga's guard was known for heavy armor and horse-cutting swords, and left a strong impression in Dutch sources.
codex.iron_man.design: Scale armor makes them tough; in melee they sweep nearby enemies. Slow-moving.
codex.iron_man.dispute: Disputed sources: some accounts say the Iron Men's armor could stop bullets, but such claims are hard to verify. The game does not adopt this (Iron Men take 1.0× musket damage) to avoid making them overpowered.
codex.musketeer_zheng.title: Musket Corps
codex.musketeer_zheng.history: The Zheng army did not rely on cold steel alone; it also fielded musket and artillery units.
codex.musketeer_zheng.design: Firing uses powder; accuracy is lower than VOC musketeers.
codex.light_cannon.title: Light Cannon
codex.light_cannon.intro: Artillery that can move with the army.
codex.light_cannon.history: The Zheng army brought many guns across the strait to bombard Fort Provintia and Fort Zeelandia.
codex.light_cannon.design: Outranged by bastions: moving straight up gets it suppressed, but placed on a battery it can suppress the fortress in turn.
codex.heavy_cannon.title: Heavy Cannon
codex.heavy_cannon.history: Late in the siege, the Zheng army massed heavy guns against Redoubt Utrecht.
codex.heavy_cannon.design: Fires only from a battery; with the battery bonus its range can exceed the bastions'.
codex.junk.title: Junk
codex.junk.intro: Chinese sailing ship, mainstay of Zheng transport and combat.
codex.junk.history: Hundreds of junks carried the army through Lakjemuyse at high tide on 30 April 1661.
codex.junk.design: Shallow draft: can use shallow channels at high tide. Carries 10 pop.
codex.fire_ship.title: Fire Ship
codex.fire_ship.intro: Small boat packed with combustibles, used to ram enemy ships.
codex.fire_ship.history: Fire attack was a traditional tactic against large sailing ships; both sides used it in the Taijiang naval battles.
codex.fire_ship.design: Explodes on contact with an enemy ship, dealing double fire damage to ships. Single use.
codex.company_worker.title: Company Worker
codex.company_worker.intro: Craftsmen and laborers employed by the East India Company.
codex.company_worker.history: Building and repair at Tayouan relied on Company workers and local labor.
codex.company_worker.design: Can gather and build. The Tayouan sandbar has almost no wood, so you depend on stockpiles and supply.
codex.musketeer_voc.title: Musketeer
codex.musketeer_voc.history: Company soldiers came from all over Europe and fought with muskets and volley tactics.
codex.musketeer_voc.design: Long range, high damage; accuracy rises when 3 or more fire together. Uses powder.
codex.pikeman.title: Pikeman
codex.pikeman.intro: Infantry with pikes who protect the musketeers.
codex.pikeman.history: 17th-century European infantry often used pikemen to protect musketeers while they reloaded.
codex.pikeman.design: +25% damage against Iron Men and rattan shield soldiers.
codex.grenadier.title: Grenadier
codex.grenadier.history: Close-range explosives were especially useful in attacking and defending fortresses.
codex.grenadier.design: Small-area blast damage; good for defending walls or sorties to wreck batteries.
codex.field_cannon.title: Field Gun
codex.field_cannon.history: The Company kept a considerable number of guns at Tayouan.
codex.field_cannon.design: Range 10; must be set up before firing.
codex.longboat.title: Longboat
codex.longboat.intro: Small rowing boat carried by larger ships.
codex.longboat.history: Thomas Pedel landed on Baxemboy by longboat for his sortie.
codex.longboat.design: Carries 6 pop; can use shallow water at high tide.
codex.yacht.title: Yacht
codex.yacht.history: The Company used yachts to sail between Tayouan, Batavia and its trading posts.
codex.yacht.design: Faster than the big ships, with weaker firepower.
codex.warship.title: Great Ship (East Indiaman)
codex.warship.intro: The Company's large armed sailing ship, such as the Hector.
codex.warship.history: On 1 May 1661, the Hector exploded and sank in the Taijiang naval battle.
codex.warship.design: Strongest firepower, can engage two targets at once, but only sails the deep main channel.
codex.village_warrior.title: Village Warrior
codex.village_warrior.history: The indigenous villages each took their own stance in the war: some accepted Zheng overtures, some aided the Company, and the Kingdom of Middag drove off the Zheng army.
codex.village_warrior.design: Cannot be trained; lent warriors who fall are not replaced. Hidden in woods; movement unaffected by terrain.
codex.zeelandia_castle.title: Fort Zeelandia
codex.zeelandia_castle.intro: The VOC's main fortress at Tayouan, today's Anping Old Fort.
codex.zeelandia_castle.history: Built in the 1620s–30s on the Ikkunshin sandbar, it was the Company's seat of rule in Taiwan. Surrendered on 1 February 1662 after a nine-month siege.
codex.zeelandia_castle.design: The strongest building on the map; if it is captured, the VOC loses.
codex.bastion.title: Bastion
codex.bastion.intro: A projecting angle of a star fort.
codex.bastion.history: Bastions let defenders fire on attackers from the flank, eliminating blind spots.
codex.bastion.design: +25% damage when two or more bastions cover the same target: a frontal assault is extremely costly.
codex.utrecht_redoubt.title: Redoubt Utrecht
codex.utrecht_redoubt.intro: A redoubt on the high ground beside Fort Zeelandia.
codex.utrecht_redoubt.history: On 25 January 1662, the Zheng army massed its guns to take Redoubt Utrecht, overlooking the fort from above.
codex.utrecht_redoubt.design: Once captured, the holder's artillery deals +50% damage to the keep.
codex.utrecht_redoubt.dispute: Disputed sources: Radis's desertion and intelligence appear only in Coyett's later writings defending himself; Chinese sources do not record it. The game presents it as a "rumor".
codex.provintia_fort.title: Fort Provintia
codex.provintia_fort.intro: The fort at Saccam, around today's Chihkan Tower.
codex.provintia_fort.history: Built after the Guo Huaiyi uprising of 1653. After the Zheng landing in 1661 it was cut off and surrendered days later.
codex.provintia_fort.design: Once captured, becomes the holder's main base and turns the Han settlers toward the Zheng.
codex.camp_zheng.title: Camp
codex.camp_zheng.history: During the siege the Zheng army built camps at Tayouan and Saccam and stayed for the long haul.
codex.camp_zheng.design: Main base and storehouse; garrisoned troops avoid disease.
codex.tuntian.title: Tuntian Fields
codex.tuntian.intro: Fields where soldiers farm to feed themselves.
codex.tuntian.history: Short of grain, Koxinga ordered each unit to take land and farm it, the beginning of the later Ming Zheng tuntian (military farms) in Taiwan.
codex.tuntian.design: Soldiers become farmer-soldiers producing grain and cannot fight meanwhile.
codex.sugar_mill.title: Sugar Mill
codex.sugar_mill.history: Under Dutch rule, many Han settlers grew rice and sugarcane for the Company around Saccam.
codex.sugar_mill.design: Provides grain daily once allied with the settlers.
codex.village_center.title: Village
codex.village_center.history: Dutch records list Siraya villages around Tainan such as Sinkan, Mattau, Soulang and Bakloan.
codex.village_center.design: Villages cannot be captured; attacking one sharply lowers goodwill.
codex.siege_works.title: Trenches, Batteries and Tunnels
codex.siege_works.history: The Zheng army approached by trenches and built batteries to bombard; Dutch records also describe mining and counter-mining by both sides.
codex.siege_works.design: Trenches block arrows and bullets, batteries extend range and reduce damage, tunnels can bring down walls.
codex.koxinga.title: Koxinga (Zheng Chenggong)
codex.koxinga.history: Born in 1624 in Hirado, Japan, son of the maritime merchant Zheng Zhilong. Rallying resistance to the Qing, he led his army against Taiwan in 1661 and died of illness there in June 1662.
codex.koxinga.design: Hero unit: nearby allies +15% attack and faster morale recovery; if he falls, the Zheng lose.
codex.hebin.title: He Bin
codex.hebin.history: He Bin served the Company as an interpreter at Tayouan, then fled to Xiamen in debt and gave Koxinga intelligence and maps of Taiwan.
codex.hebin.design: Grants the "He Bin's Chart" technology automatically at the start of Chapter 1.
codex.coyett.title: Frederick Coyett
codex.coyett.history: Blamed by the Company and exiled after the siege failed, he later published 't Verwaerloosde Formosa (Neglected Formosa) in his own defense, blaming Batavia's neglect for the defeat.
codex.coyett.design: Hero unit: nearby buildings take -20% damage and garrison morale falls more slowly.
codex.pedel.title: Thomas Pedel
codex.pedel.history: On 1 May 1661 he led about 240 musketeers in a sortie on Baxemboy and was routed; he and 118 men were killed.
codex.pedel.design: VOC hero in Chapter 1, can be killed; his death drops fort morale by 20.
codex.valentyn.title: Jacobus Valentijn
codex.valentyn.history: Fort Provintia's garrison of about 140 surrendered after being cut off for several days.
codex.valentyn.design: In Chapter 2 the VOC side may negotiate surrender, keeping its troops and withdrawing to Tayouan.
codex.caeuw.title: Jacob Caeuw
codex.caeuw.history: In summer 1661 he brought about 12 ships and 700 men to the rescue; after the failed counterattack in September, he left Taiwan in December, claiming to seek contact with the Qing court, and returned to Batavia.
codex.caeuw.design: Relief commander in Chapter 3; his departure at the start of Chapter 4 lowers fort morale.
codex.hambroek.title: Antonius Hambroek
codex.hambroek.history: After his capture he was sent into the fort to urge surrender; Coyett refused, and he was killed after returning to the Zheng camp.
codex.hambroek.design: Cutscene figure, not playable; the game records his fate in a single neutral line.
codex.radis.title: Hans Jurgen Radis
codex.radis.intro: German sergeant who deserted (recorded only in Dutch sources).
codex.radis.history: According to Coyett's side, after deserting he pointed out to the Zheng army that Redoubt Utrecht was Fort Zeelandia's weak point.
codex.radis.design: Presented as a "rumor" in Chapter 4: reveals the area around Redoubt Utrecht.
codex.radis.dispute: Disputed sources: Radis's desertion and intelligence appear only in Coyett's later writings defending himself; Chinese sources do not record it. The game presents it as a "rumor".
codex.tayouan.title: Tayouan
codex.tayouan.intro: A sandbar around today's Anping, Tainan.
codex.tayouan.history: The Company built Fort Zeelandia and the town of Tayouan here. One theory holds that the name "Taiwan" comes from Tayouan.
codex.tayouan.design: Almost no wood; the VOC must rely on stockpiles and supply by sea.
codex.baxemboy.title: Baxemboy
codex.baxemboy.history: Where Thomas Pedel made his sortie on 1 May 1661.
codex.luermen.title: Lakjemuyse (Luermen)
codex.luermen.intro: A shallow channel north of Baxemboy.
codex.luermen.history: The Dutch thought large ships could not pass, but the Zheng army entered the Taijiang inner sea here at high tide.
codex.luermen.design: Junks can pass only at high tide; at low tide they run aground.
codex.taijiang.title: Taijiang (inner sea)
codex.taijiang.intro: A lagoon since silted up and gone.
codex.taijiang.history: In the 17th century the waters off Tainan were a shallow inner sea; from the 19th century it gradually silted into land.
codex.taijiang.design: Mostly shallow water; the tide decides who can pass.
codex.saccam.title: Saccam
codex.saccam.history: Site of Fort Provintia, surrounded by the farms of many Han settlers.
codex.saccam.design: Farmland and sugar mills of the Han Chinese settlers are here.
codex.heliao.title: Heliao Harbor

codex.middag.intro: A multi-village alliance in central Taiwan.
codex.middag.history: When the Zheng army sent troops north to open military farms, Middag first welcomed and then attacked them, wiping out about 1,500 Zheng soldiers.
codex.middag.design: Shown as a northern event: sending large numbers of troops north may trigger an ambush.
codex.numbers.title: Troop and casualty figures
codex.numbers.history: Common account: about 25,000 Zheng troops crossed the strait, with about 6,000 actually advancing to the fort; Fort Zeelandia held 1,733 people, about 905 of them soldiers. Roughly half of the Zheng personnel in Taiwan died or deserted, most from disease.
codex.numbers.design: The game scales forces at roughly 1:10 and uses a population cap rather than real headcounts.
codex.numbers.dispute: Disputed: troop and casualty figures vary by source; Dutch records, Chinese sources and later research all give different estimates.
codex.dates.title: Dates
codex.dates.intro: Chinese sources mostly use the lunar calendar; English sources sometimes mix the two.
codex.dates.history: For example, Fort Provintia surrendered on the 4th day of the 4th month (lunar calendar), i.e. 4 May.
codex.dates.design: The game uses the Western calendar throughout, following Andrade's conversions.
codex.dates.dispute: Disputed: Western–lunar conversions and the dates recorded in different documents sometimes disagree; before release they should be checked one by one against the Chinese translation of the Zeelandia Dagregisters.
dispute.iron_armor: Disputed: some accounts claim the Iron Men's armor could stop bullets, but such claims are hard to verify. The game does not adopt this (Iron Men take 1.0× musket damage) to avoid making them too strong.
dispute.radis: Disputed: Radis's defection and the intelligence he provided appear only in Coyett's later self-defense; Chinese sources do not mention it. The game presents it as a "rumor".

tutorial.camera.title: Moving the camera
tutorial.camera.text: Move the camera with the arrow keys, by moving the mouse to the screen edge, or by holding the middle mouse button and dragging; the wheel zooms. On a laptop touchpad you can turn on "Touchpad mode" in Settings: two-finger scroll pans, pinch to zoom. You can also click the minimap in the lower left to jump there. Try moving the camera some distance away.
tutorial.select.title: Selecting units
tutorial.select.text: The camera is back at the camp in Saccam. Left-click a soldier: the selection panel below shows its health, morale, attack and armor.
tutorial.box.title: Box selection
tutorial.box.text: Hold left-click and drag a box around the rattan shield troops and archers together (at least 5). Press Ctrl + a number key to save them as a group, then press that number to recall them.
tutorial.move.title: Moving
tutorial.move.text: With troops selected, right-click the ground to move (no right button: Alt + left-click, or hold left-click for half a second; in touchpad mode just left-click the ground). Bring the troops to the yellow flag.
tutorial.gather.title: Gathering
tutorial.gather.text: Laborers gather and build. Select laborers (box selection works) and right-click the woods to the east to start chopping. Wood is carried back to the camp automatically.
tutorial.resources.title: Resources
tutorial.resources.text: The resource bar at the top shows grain, wood, powder, deerskin and pop. Every unit eats grain each day; when grain runs out, the grain icon flashes red and the whole army's morale drops. Wait until wood is back above 260.
tutorial.build.title: Building a barracks
tutorial.build.text: Select laborers and press B to open the build menu (or click "Build" in the command panel at the lower right), choose "Barracks", then left-click open ground near the camp to place it. Green means you can build; red means you can't.
tutorial.wait_build.title: Waiting for construction
tutorial.wait_build.text: The laborers are building. More laborers build faster: select laborers and right-click the construction site.
tutorial.train.title: Training soldiers
tutorial.train.text: Click the finished barracks; the command panel at the lower right lists trainable units and their costs. Train one rattan shield soldier. Right-click the ground to set a rally point.
tutorial.tide.title: Tides
tutorial.tide.text: The ring at the upper right is the tide: at rising and high tide, junks can cross shallow water; at low tide, ships left in the shallows run aground. Select the junk by the shore and sail it into the inner sea to the west while the tide is rising (if it is ebbing, wait for the ring to turn to rising tide).
tutorial.combat.title: Combat
tutorial.combat.text: Dutch pikemen have appeared! Select troops and right-click an enemy to attack; press A then click the ground to "attack-move", fighting any enemy along the way. Pikemen counter rattan shield troops and Iron Men; archers can wear them down from range.
tutorial.diplomacy.title: Diplomacy
tutorial.diplomacy.text: There are more than two sides on the island. The camera has moved to Sinkan: select a village to see its goodwill toward each side and the reasons for recent changes. You need your own units in the village's territory to give gifts or win it over (press G to give grain). At goodwill 80 or more and 20 ahead of your rival, the village joins you.
tutorial.pause.title: Pause and speed
tutorial.pause.text: Press Space to pause: you can still give orders while paused. + / − adjust game speed. Press Space now.
tutorial.done.title: Done!
tutorial.done.text: You've learned the basics. In the real campaigns you'll also face the crossfire of bastions (you need trenches and gun batteries to besiege them), disease, supply lines and typhoons. The Codex explains every unit and its history. Keep practicing here, or press the button below to return to the Main menu.
ch4.end.utrecht_held: With Redoubt Utrecht commanding the heights, Fort Zeelandia can no longer hold. Coyett opens the gates to negotiate.

history.mudan1: Battle of Stone Gate · History: On 22 May 1874, a Japanese detachment advanced up the Sichongxi to attack Stone Gate, while Paiwan warriors fired from the cliffs on both sides. The Japanese sent men up the cliffs to strike from the flank; Aruqu, chief of Mudan, and his son were killed, and Stone Gate fell. In early June the Japanese advanced in three columns and burned Mudan, Kuskus, Ninai and other villages; the people withdrew deep into the mountains, and several chiefs later made peace with the Japanese. Few Japanese died in battle, but more than 500 reportedly died of malaria and other diseases. On 31 October, Qing and Japan signed the Peking Agreement: the Qing paid 500,000 taels of silver, and the treaty called the expedition a "just act to protect its people". Japanese troops withdrew in December. Japan later used this to strengthen its claim over Ryukyu, annexing it as Okinawa Prefecture in 1879.
cut.mudan1_intro.title: Stone Gate · 1874
cut.mudan1_intro.1: In the winter of 1871, a Ryukyuan ship from Miyako Island struck a reef in Bayao Bay. More than sixty people who came ashore walked into the lands of Kuskus; unable to understand one another and mutually suspicious, 54 were killed. The 12 survivors were taken in by Han villagers of Baoli and eventually sent home to Ryukyu.
cut.mudan1_intro.2: Three years later, in the name of "seeking justice for the Ryukyuans", Japan sent troops to southern Taiwan without the Qing court's consent. In May 1874, Saigō Jūdō landed at Sialiao with more than three thousand men: the first overseas military expedition of Meiji Japan.
cut.mudan1_intro.3: For the Paiwan, this was outsiders with guns and cannon forcing their way into ancestral lands. Aruqu, chief of Mudan, gathered warriors from the communities and laid an ambush on the cliffs where the Sichongxi narrows into the "Stone Gate".
cut.mudan1_intro.4: On 22 May, the Japanese came up the stream. Behind the lines, the villagers were packing their belongings and withdrawing into the mountains.

codex.paiwan_hunter.title: Paiwan hunter (matchlock)
codex.paiwan_hunter.intro: Hunters who know the mountain forests, firing matchlocks from high ground and from among the trees.
codex.paiwan_hunter.history: In the 19th century, the Paiwan of the Hengchun Peninsula obtained matchlocks and powder through trade with Han Chinese, using them for hunting and guarding their territory. At Stone Gate, warriors fired down into the valley from the cliffs on both sides.
codex.paiwan_hunter.design: Hidden in forest (enemies see them only within 2 tiles); +1 range on mountains and hills. Matchlocks reload slowly, and the smoke from firing reveals their position for 3 seconds. They know the mountain trails and move far faster than the Japanese in the mountains.
codex.paiwan_warrior.title: Paiwan warrior
codex.paiwan_warrior.intro: Warriors fighting at close quarters with machetes.
codex.paiwan_warrior.history: Paiwan men learned to hunt and travel the mountains from childhood. Against Japanese soldiers climbing the cliffs, hand-to-hand fighting was the last means of holding the heights.
codex.paiwan_warrior.design: Fast, hidden in forest, knows the mountain trails; good at meeting enemies climbing onto the heights, but charging into the open valley gets them pinned down by rifles.
codex.paiwan_family.title: Villagers
codex.paiwan_family.intro: The elders, women and children of each community.
codex.paiwan_family.history: After the Japanese entered the mountains, the people of each community withdrew deep into the mountains with their belongings; the village houses were burned in June.
codex.paiwan_family.design: Do not fight and are not targeted. After the start they automatically retreat into the mountains to the northeast (scripted).
codex.japan_infantry.title: Japanese infantry
codex.japan_infantry.intro: Regular infantry of the Meiji army, armed with breech-loading rifles.
codex.japan_infantry.history: The expedition was built mainly around regulars such as those of the Kumamoto Garrison. Breech-loaders outranged and outfired matchlocks, but in unfamiliar mountains the soldiers could not see marksmen hidden in the forest.
codex.japan_infantry.design: Range 7, fast rate of fire; cannot see enemies in forest until they fire and give off smoke or come within 2 tiles. Very slow in the mountains.
codex.japan_volunteer.title: Volunteer corps
codex.japan_volunteer.intro: Samurai-class (shizoku) volunteers fighting mainly with swords.
codex.japan_volunteer.history: Saigō Jūdō recruited a volunteer unit of former Satsuma-domain shizoku around Kagoshima to accompany the expedition.
codex.japan_volunteer.design: Melee; good for scaling cliffs and clearing ambushers from the heights.
codex.aruqu.title: Aruqu
codex.aruqu.history: At the Battle of Stone Gate on 22 May 1874, Aruqu led warriors from the communities in holding Stone Gate and was killed together with his son. The Chinese-character rendering of his name varies slightly between sources.
codex.aruqu.design: Hero unit: nearby villagers get +15% attack and faster morale recovery. His survival is the Paiwan side's optional objective.
codex.sakuma.title: Sakuma Samata
codex.sakuma.intro: Japanese army officer who led the attacking troops at Stone Gate.
codex.sakuma.history: A native of Chōshū. He joined the 1874 expedition and directed the cliff-climbing flank attack at Stone Gate. More than thirty years later, as the fifth Governor-General of Taiwan, he pushed the "Five-Year Riban Plan" (aboriginal-control plan) and personally commanded the 1914 Truku War.
codex.sakuma.design: Hero unit: nearby troops get +10% attack.
codex.m_saigo.title: Saigō Jūdō
codex.m_saigo.intro: "Commander of Taiwan Aboriginal Territory Affairs", supreme commander of the expedition.
codex.m_saigo.history: Younger brother of Saigō Takamori. In 1874, while there was still dissent within the government, he led the force out from Nagasaki, landed at Sialiao, and set up his headquarters at Kameyama.
codex.m_saigo.design: Does not appear in this chapter; the Japanese camp and the later main force represent the expedition he commanded.
codex.m_legendre.title: Charles W. Le Gendre
codex.m_legendre.intro: Former U.S. consul at Amoy and adviser to the Japanese.
codex.m_legendre.history: After the Rover incident of 1867, he reached an agreement with Tauketok, paramount chief of the eighteen communities of Lower Langqiao, to aid shipwreck survivors. From 1872 he was employed by Japan's Foreign Ministry, supplying geography and intelligence on southern Taiwan and arguing strongly for an expedition.
codex.m_legendre.design: Does not appear in this chapter.
codex.m_shimen.title: Stone Gate
codex.m_shimen.intro: A narrow valley on the upper Sichongxi, hemmed in by cliffs on both sides.
codex.m_shimen.history: The only route into Mudan and the other villages. Today a Stone Gate battlefield memorial stands near Shimen Village, Mudan Township, Pingtung County.
codex.m_shimen.design: The valley floor is at most 5 tiles wide; the heights on both sides are wooded and command the valley. Going around the mountain is at least twice as far as going through the gorge.
codex.m_mudan.title: Mudan (Sinvaudjan)
codex.m_mudan.intro: A Paiwan village in the mountains of the Hengchun Peninsula.
codex.m_mudan.history: Closely tied to neighboring villages such as Kuskus and Ninai; historically called the "Mudan group". Today Mudan Township, Pingtung County.
codex.m_mudan.design: In this chapter Mudan is the starting point of the villagers' withdrawal; the Japanese do not attack the village itself until June.
codex.m_kuskus.title: Kuskus
codex.m_kuskus.intro: A Paiwan village southeast of Mudan.
codex.m_kuskus.history: In 1871, the Ryukyuan shipwreck survivors came ashore and walked into the lands of Kuskus.
codex.m_kuskus.design: Warriors from Kuskus arrive as reinforcements 2 min 30 s after the start; warriors from Ninai arrive at 5 minutes.
codex.m_sialiao.title: Sialiao and Checheng
codex.m_sialiao.intro: Han Chinese and Pingpu settlements around the mouth of the Sichongxi.
codex.m_sialiao.history: The Japanese landed at Sialiao, camped at Kameyama, and hired local guides and porters. Hakka villages such as Tongpu and Baoli lay downstream in the valley; Yang Youwang, who took in the Ryukyuan survivors in 1871, was a resident of Baoli.
codex.m_sialiao.design: Neutral settlements; they do not fight.
codex.m_1871.title: Bayao Bay Incident (1871)
codex.m_1871.intro: Accounts of how the Ryukyuan shipwreck survivors were killed differ.
codex.m_1871.history: Common account: 69 people were aboard, 3 drowned and 66 came ashore; villagers gave them water and food, but the Ryukyuans left during the night, and when they were caught, 54 were killed and 12 survived. Interpretations of why differ, including misunderstandings of language and custom, and suspicion that they were enemies.
codex.m_1871.design: Shown as a cutscene; the player does not control this event.
codex.m_1871.dispute: Disputed: the account comes mainly from survivors and later Japanese records; Paiwan oral perspectives have only recently received more attention.
codex.m_numbers.title: Forces and casualties in 1874
codex.m_numbers.history: Common account: the Japanese sent about 3,600 men. Records of casualties at Stone Gate differ; about a dozen or so Paiwan were killed (including Aruqu and his son). About a dozen or so Japanese died in battle, and about 560 reportedly died of disease.
codex.m_numbers.design: The game scales forces at roughly 1:4 and compresses a day into a minute: each day a few Japanese soldiers fall ill with malaria.
codex.m_numbers.dispute: Disputed: Japanese official records, the embedded journalist and Paiwan oral accounts do not fully agree on the numbers or events.

history.mudan2: Three-Column Advance · History: From 1 June, the Japanese entered the mountains in three columns, and on the 2nd and 3rd burned the houses of Mudan, Kuskus, Ninai and other villages, facing scattered ambushes along the way. The people had withdrawn deep into the mountains beforehand, and the Japanese never found anyone to fight a decisive battle with. The Japanese then set up camps in the mountains and at Kameyama, but disease spread rapidly; from July, with other communities acting as intermediaries, the chiefs gradually made contact with the Japanese to negotiate peace.
cut.mudan2_intro.title: Three Columns · June 1874
cut.mudan2_intro.1: After the Battle of Stone Gate, the Japanese regrouped around Kameyama and Stone Gate. In early June, Saigō Jūdō ordered three columns into the mountains: one through Stone Gate straight to Mudan, one from the north against Ninai, and one from the south against Kuskus.
cut.mudan2_intro.2: The Japanese outnumbered the warriors several times over; but the mountain paths were narrow, the forest dense, and malaria in the camps was getting worse.
cut.mudan2_intro.3: The communities knew they could not stop three columns. The elders, women and children had to leave the villages before the Japanese arrived; the warriors laid ambushes on the mountain paths to slow them down.
codex.m_routes.title: Routes of the three columns
codex.m_routes.intro: The Japanese three-pronged attack of early June.
codex.m_routes.history: Common account: the northern column attacked Ninai from Fenggang, the central column went through Stone Gate to Mudan, and the southern column attacked Kuskus from around Zhushe. Accounts differ slightly on each column's commanders and strength.
codex.m_routes.design: The map is schematic: the relative directions of the three routes match history, but distances are greatly compressed. The southern column starts from around Baoli instead.
codex.m_routes.dispute: Disputed: Japanese records and later research do not fully agree on each column's starting point, strength and dates.
codex.m_nunai.title: Ninai
codex.m_nunai.intro: A Paiwan village near Mudan, part of the "Mudan group".
codex.m_nunai.history: Burned by the Japanese in June 1874 along with Mudan, Kuskus and other villages. Its name in the Paiwan language and exact location remain to be verified.
codex.m_nunai.design: Target of the Japanese northern column in Chapter 2.

history.penghu1: Bazhao · History: On 10 July 1683 (16th day of the 6th month, lunar calendar), the Qing fleet, hampered by the wind, held back; only Lan Li charged into the Zheng fleet with 7 ships. The second wave of Qing ships met the rising tide and some were swept toward the shore, while the Zheng fleet enveloped them on both wings. Coming to the rescue, Shi Lang was surrounded by Lin Sheng and wounded in the right eye by musket fire (he was not blinded); a cannonball shattered Lin Sheng's left leg. The Qing fell back to the Xiyu–Bazhao area to regroup, and Liu Guoxuan reported a victory to Taiwan.
cut.penghu1_intro.title: Penghu · 1683
cut.penghu1_intro.1: In 1681 Zheng Jing died of illness. A coup in Tungning put the young Zheng Keshuang on the throne, with real power in the hands of Feng Xifan and Liu Guoxuan. That same year, the Kangxi Emperor reappointed Shi Lang as admiral of the Fujian navy.
cut.penghu1_intro.2: Shi Lang had once been one of Koxinga's officers. After he broke with Koxinga, his father and brother were killed, and he went over to the Qing. Thirty years later, he returned to these waters with more than two hundred warships.
cut.penghu1_intro.3: Liu Guoxuan held Penghu in strength, building forts and gun positions at Niangmagong, Fengguiwei and elsewhere, and low walls along the shore. Summer was typhoon season, and he judged that the Qing would not dare cross the strait then.
cut.penghu1_intro.4: On 8 July the Qing fleet sailed from Tongshan. Two days later, its sails appeared off Niangmagong.

penghu2.end.history: Niangmagong falls and the Zheng fleet is scattered; Liu Guoxuan retreats to Taiwan through Houmen. As in history.
penghu2.end.liu_sunk: Niangmagong falls, and Liu Guoxuan's flagship fails to escape. Worse than in history.
penghu2.end.shi_sunk: Shi Lang's flagship is sunk, and the Qing offensive collapses.
penghu2.end.repulsed: Having lost more than half their ships, the Qing fall back to Bazhao as typhoon season approaches.
penghu2.end.held: Niangmagong holds. With typhoon season approaching, the Qing are forced to withdraw.
history.penghu2: Niangmagong · History: On 16 July (22nd day of the 6th month, lunar calendar), Shi Lang led the main attack on Niangmagong with a central force of 56 ships in 8 squadrons, five ships attacking each enemy ship. A left force of 50 ships struck Niuxin Bay to mislead the Zheng side about the landing site; a right force of 50 attacked Jilong Islet and Sijiao Islet; about 80 ships were held in reserve. According to some accounts, a northwest wind in the morning briefly gave the Zheng fleet the upper hand, but when the wind turned south at noon the Qing launched an all-out counterattack. The Zheng fleet was routed, and Liu Guoxuan escaped to Taiwan through Houmen to the north with a few dozen small boats. Shi Lang reported 329 Qing dead and about 12,000 Zheng dead (possibly exaggerated). In September Zheng Keshuang submitted his surrender; in October Shi Lang arrived in Taiwan to accept it, and the following year the Qing court established Taiwan Prefecture.
cut.penghu2_intro.title: Niangmagong · The Decisive Battle
cut.penghu2_intro.1: After the first battle, Shi Lang regrouped his fleet at Bazhao and waited for reinforcements. Six days later, he divided the fleet into three forces.
cut.penghu2_intro.2: He led the center himself, straight at Niangmagong; the left force attacked Niuxin Bay, and the right force Jilong Islet and Sijiao Islet. Five ships attacked each enemy ship, a tactic later called the "five-petal plum blossom."
cut.penghu2_intro.3: At dawn, a northwest wind is blowing over the sea.

codex.qing_niaochuan.title: Large Bird Ship
codex.qing_niaochuan.intro: The large main warship of the Qing navy.
codex.qing_niaochuan.history: Of the 238 ships in Shi Lang's expedition, about 70 were large bird ships; being fast, they served as the vanguard in the first battle.
codex.qing_niaochuan.design: Deep water only; strong firepower and can fire at two targets at once.
codex.qing_ganzeng.title: Ganzeng Ship
codex.qing_ganzeng.intro: The Qing navy's most numerous medium warship.
codex.qing_ganzeng.history: About 103 of the expedition's ships were ganzeng ships.
codex.qing_ganzeng.design: Can enter shallow water at high tide; balanced attack and defense.
codex.qing_shuangfan.title: Two-Masted Ju Ship
codex.qing_shuangfan.history: About 65 of the expedition's ships were two-masted ju ships (sources write the name slightly differently).
codex.qing_shuangfan.design: Fastest ship, weak firepower; good for flanking and pursuit.
codex.tn_paochuan.title: Large Gunboat (Tungning)
codex.tn_paochuan.intro: The large warship of the Tungning navy.
codex.tn_paochuan.history: The Zheng navy had gunboats large and small, ocean-going ships, two-masted ships and more. Records of its numbers vary: about 200 ships, or only 40–50.
codex.tn_paochuan.design: Comparable to the Qing large bird ship: the two sides differed in numbers, terrain and shore guns, not technology.
codex.tn_paochuan.dispute: Disputed: estimates of Zheng troop strength range from 20,000 to 30,000, and ship counts vary even more widely.
codex.tn_fort.title: Forts and Batteries
codex.tn_fort.intro: Fortifications Liu Guoxuan built along the coast of Penghu.
codex.tn_fort.history: Forts were built at Niangmagong, Fengguiwei, Sijiao Islet and Jilong Islet; batteries at Dongshi, Xishi, Neiqian, Waiqian, Xiyutou and Niuxinshan; low walls manned with muskets were also built along the shore to stop Qing landings.
codex.tn_fort.design: Crossfire bonus when two or more cover the same ship. This game shows only the naval battle; the shore walls and landing fights are not included.
codex.shi_lang.title: Shi Lang
codex.shi_lang.intro: Admiral of the Qing Fujian navy and commander of the conquest of Taiwan.
codex.shi_lang.history: Originally one of Koxinga's officers; after he broke with Koxinga, his father and brother were killed and he went over to the Qing. Reappointed admiral of the Fujian navy in 1681, he took Penghu in 1683 and accepted Zheng Keshuang's surrender; the following year he petitioned the throne to keep Taiwan.
codex.shi_lang.design: Flagship hero: nearby ships +15% attack. In chapter 1 he withdraws when badly damaged (as in history); if his flagship sinks, the Qing side loses.
codex.shi_lang.dispute: Disputed: opinions of Shi Lang are sharply divided; some see him as a turncoat who betrayed his lord, others as a man of great merit. This game presents his life and motives without passing judgment.
codex.liu_guoxuan.title: Liu Guoxuan
codex.liu_guoxuan.intro: Tungning general, commander of the Penghu garrison.
codex.liu_guoxuan.history: After Zheng Jing's death he shared power in Tungning with Feng Xifan. In 1683 he held Penghu in strength; after losing the decisive battle he retreated to Taiwan through Houmen, and later surrendered to the Qing together with Zheng Keshuang.
codex.liu_guoxuan.design: Flagship hero: nearby ships +15% attack. In chapter 2, once Niangmagong falls he tries to escape through Houmen; if his flagship sinks, the result is worse than in history.
codex.lan_li.title: Lan Li
codex.lan_li.history: In the first battle he charged into the Zheng line with 7 ships to cover the Qing withdrawal, and was wounded in the abdomen.
codex.lin_sheng.title: Lin Sheng
codex.lin_sheng.history: With Jiang Sheng he commanded the Zheng fleet in the first battle and surrounded Shi Lang's ship; a cannonball shattered his left leg during the fighting.
codex.p_penghu.title: Penghu Islands
codex.p_penghu.intro: An archipelago in the Taiwan Strait, the gateway to Tungning.
codex.p_penghu.history: Niangmagong (today's Magong) was the main harbor; Xiyu, Baisha and Fengguiwei enclose the inner sea. Bazhao (today's Wang'an) to the south was the Qing anchorage.
codex.p_penghu.design: The map is schematic: the islands' relative positions match history, but distances are greatly compressed.
codex.p_houmen.title: Houmen
codex.p_houmen.intro: The channel between Xiyu and Baisha leading north.
codex.p_houmen.history: After losing the decisive battle, Liu Guoxuan led his remaining forces back to Taiwan through Houmen to the north.
codex.p_houmen.design: A deep channel for large ships runs along the east side; the west side is reefs and shoals.
codex.p_numbers.title: Forces and Casualties in 1683
codex.p_numbers.intro: The figures come mainly from the Qing side.
codex.p_numbers.history: Qing: about 21,000–24,000 men and 238 ships (other accounts give 20,000 men and 300 ships, or 60,000 men and 600 ships). Shi Lang reported 329 Qing dead and 1,800 wounded; Zheng losses of about 12,000 dead (about 14,000 including the first battle), about 5,000 surrendered, and over 190 ships lost.
codex.p_numbers.design: The game scales ship numbers at roughly 1:5.
codex.p_numbers.dispute: Disputed: the casualty figures come from Shi Lang's own report, which may exaggerate his success and understate his losses; the dates in the English trading post's records also differ from the Qing account.
codex.p_wind.title: The Wind on the Day of Battle
codex.p_wind.intro: Northwest wind in the morning, turning south at noon.
codex.p_wind.history: According to some accounts, a northwest wind blew in the early morning of the decisive battle, briefly giving the downwind Zheng fleet the upper hand; at noon it turned south, favoring the Qing, and Shi Lang launched an all-out counterattack. Other accounts note that typhoons were common in this season, which is why Liu Guoxuan judged the Qing would not come.
codex.p_wind.design: Chapter 2 opens with a northwest wind, which turns south after 4 minutes. Sailing ships are up to 45% faster with the wind and up to 45% slower against it.
codex.p_wind.dispute: Disputed: details of the wind shift appear only in some accounts and could not be checked against other sources.

history.yiwei1: Aodi · History: On 29 May 1895 the Imperial Guard Division landed at Aodi, crossed Sandiaoling, defeated the defenders at Ruifang on 2 June and took Keelung on the 3rd; that same day Li Jingfang and Kabayama Sukenori completed the handover at sea. On the 6th President Tang Jingsong fled to Xiamen in disguise, order in Taipei collapsed, and on the 7th the Japanese entered Taipei without a fight.
cut.yiwei1_intro.title: Cession · 1895
cut.yiwei1_intro.1: In April 1895, defeated in the First Sino-Japanese War, the Qing signed the Treaty of Shimonoseki, ceding Taiwan and Penghu to Japan. When the news arrived, Taiwan's gentry were outraged.
cut.yiwei1_intro.2: In May, officials and gentry in Taipei proclaimed the "Republic of Formosa," naming Governor Tang Jingsong president and Qiu Fengjia vice president and militia commissioner, adopting a yellow tiger on a blue field as the flag, and vowing to resist the cession.
cut.yiwei1_intro.3: The Republic's army was mostly troops left behind by the Qing, long unpaid and unevenly disciplined; those truly willing to fight for their homes were the militias organized locally.
cut.yiwei1_intro.4: On 29 May the Japanese Imperial Guard Division landed at Aodi on the northeast coast.

yiwei2.msg.hsinchu: Japanese supply carts reach Hsinchu and set up a depot in the city.
yiwei2.end.history: Supply columns are ambushed again and again, but the Japanese take Miaoli at a cost. As in history.
yiwei2.end.swift: The Japanese take Miaoli; the militias failed to cut their supply.

yiwei2.end.repulsed: Out of supplies and with heavy casualties, the Japanese fall back north of Hsinchu.
yiwei2.end.held: The Japanese fail to take Miaoli within 14 minutes.
history.yiwei2: Taoyuan–Hsinchu–Miaoli · History: The Japanese occupied Hsinchu on 22 June, but Hakka militias around Taoyuan and Hsinchu attacked them constantly. At the Battle of Longenpu on 13 July, a Japanese supply column was almost wiped out; at the Battle of Fenshuilun on the 16th, Japanese reinforcements broke the siege. Jiang Shaozu was captured and took poison. From late July the Japanese burned villages in sweeps between Taipei and Hsinchu, causing heavy civilian casualties (for disputed figures, see the Codex). On 14 August the Japanese entered Miaoli.
cut.yiwei2_intro.title: The Militias · Summer 1895
cut.yiwei2_intro.1: After entering Taipei, the Japanese pushed south. Most of the Republic's regular troops had scattered; in their path stood Hakka militias raised by Wu Tangxing, Jiang Shaozu, Xu Xiang and others.
cut.yiwei2_intro.2: The militias knew the hills and bamboo groves; they avoided open battle and struck at the long Japanese supply columns.
cut.yiwei2_intro.3: Japanese supplies depended on large numbers of porters pushing carts and carrying loads all the way from Taipei to the front.
scenario.yiwei3.name: Baguashan
yiwei3.obj.take: Within 12 minutes, cross the Dadu River, destroy the Baguashan Battery and occupy Changhua (6 troops, no defenders, 30 seconds)
yiwei3.obj.hold: Hold Baguashan and Changhua for 12 minutes, or reduce the Japanese force below 14
yiwei3.obj.leaders: (Optional) Wu Tangxing and Wu Pengnian must both survive
yiwei3.msg.night: Under cover of night, the Japanese begin wading across the Dadu River.
yiwei3.end.history: Baguashan and Changhua fall, and the combined northern and southern forces scatter. As in history.
yiwei3.end.rout: Baguashan falls and nearly all its defenders are killed. Worse than in history.
yiwei3.end.repulsed: With heavy casualties below Baguashan, the Japanese fall back to the north bank of the Dadu River.
yiwei3.end.held: The Japanese fail to take Baguashan and Changhua within 12 minutes.
history.yiwei3: Baguashan · History: From 27 August the Japanese shelled Baguashan with mountain guns. Before dawn on the 28th, the Imperial Guard Division crossed the Dadu River by night and at daybreak launched a general assault on the Baguashan Battery and Changhua, taking them after about eight hours. Wu Tangxing, Wu Pengnian and Yan Yunlong were killed, and the survivors fell back to Chiayi and Lukang. It was the largest pitched battle of the war. Afterward the Japanese advance stalled for about a month because of disease.
cut.yiwei3_intro.title: Baguashan · August 1895
cut.yiwei3_intro.1: After Miaoli fell, the militias from the north joined the Black Flag Army sent by Liu Yongfu, forming the "combined northern and southern forces," and held Baguashan east of Changhua.
cut.yiwei3_intro.2: Krupp breech-loading guns on the hill overlooked the Dadu River; as long as Baguashan held, the Japanese could not get past Changhua.
cut.yiwei3_intro.3: Before dawn on 28 August, under cover of night, the Japanese begin wading across the Dadu River.
scenario.yiwei4.name: Tainan
yiwei4.obj.take: Within 15 minutes, encircle Tainan from three directions and occupy it (8 troops, no defenders, 30 seconds); disease steadily weakens your units
yiwei4.obj.hold: Hold Tainan for 15 minutes, or reduce the Japanese force below 12

yiwei4.msg.landings: The Japanese land at Budaizui and Fangliao!
yiwei4.msg.liu_fled: Liu Yongfu leaves Tainan in disguise and sails for the mainland.
yiwei4.end.history: Encircled by Japanese forces from three directions, Tainan opens its gates; Liu Yongfu leaves for the mainland. As in history.
yiwei4.end.liu_fled: Liu Yongfu leaves for the mainland, and Tainan opens its gates. As in history.
yiwei4.end.liu_dead: Tainan falls and Liu Yongfu is killed. Worse than in history.
yiwei4.end.repulsed: Disease and casualties leave the Japanese unable to complete the encirclement; the offensive stalls.
yiwei4.end.held: The Japanese fail to take Tainan within 15 minutes.
history.yiwei4: Tainan · History: Chiayi fell on 9 October. On the 10th and 11th the 4th Mixed Brigade landed at Budaizui and the 2nd Division at Fangliao, encircling Tainan from three directions together with the Imperial Guard Division from the north. Liu Yongfu offered a conditional surrender, which was refused, and on 20 October he left for the mainland in disguise; that same day Japanese troops burned villages and killed villagers around Xiaolong. On the 21st the Japanese entered Tainan. Several hundred Japanese were killed in action and several thousand died of disease; Prince Kitashirakawa Yoshihisa died in Tainan on 28 October. Armed resistance to Japanese rule continued in many places for years afterward, and indigenous resistance went on for about twenty more years.
cut.yiwei4_intro.title: Tainan · October 1895
cut.yiwei4_intro.1: After Baguashan, the Japanese halted in Changhua for a month: cholera, malaria and beriberi felled far more men than combat did.
cut.yiwei4_intro.2: In October the Japanese pushed south again and took Chiayi, while forces landed from the sea at Budaizui and Fangliao, encircling Tainan from three directions.
cut.yiwei4_intro.3: In Tainan, the Republic's second president, Liu Yongfu, had only the Black Flag Army and local militias left.

codex.jp95_guard.title: Guard Infantry / Japanese Infantry
codex.jp95_guard.intro: Regular Japanese army infantry armed with Murata rifles.
codex.jp95_guard.history: The Imperial Guard Division landed first; later the 2nd Division and the 4th Mixed Brigade landed in the south. The Japanese force numbered nearly 50,000 officers and men plus more than 20,000 porters, but disease greatly thinned its ranks.
codex.jp95_guard.design: Range 7, fast rate of fire; cannot see militia hidden in hills and forests. In chapter 4, disease is deadlier than combat.
codex.jp95_cart.title: Supply Cart (Porters)
codex.jp95_cart.intro: Porters and carts carrying food and ammunition for the Japanese army.
codex.jp95_cart.history: The Japanese conscripted more than 20,000 porters. At the Battle of Longenpu on 13 July 1895, a Japanese supply column was almost wiped out by the militia.
codex.jp95_cart.design: Chapter 2: Japanese units must stay within 9 tiles of a depot or supply cart, or their morale drops every second. Carts cannot fight and are the militia's top target.
codex.fm_regular.title: Republic's Qing Troops
codex.fm_regular.intro: Former Qing troops (Cantonese braves and others) taken over by the Republic of Formosa.
codex.fm_regular.history: Mostly units left behind by the Qing or hastily recruited, unpaid and unevenly disciplined; after Tang Jingsong fled, the Taipei garrison disintegrated and some even turned to looting.
codex.fm_regular.design: Numerous but average in combat; in chapter 1, when Tang Jingsong flees, the troops in Taipei scatter.
codex.fm_blackflag.title: Black Flag Army
codex.fm_blackflag.intro: Liu Yongfu's force, famous from the Sino-French War.
codex.fm_blackflag.history: Liu Yongfu was ordered to Taiwan and stationed in Tainan. The Black Flag Army carried Winchester, Mauser and other rifles; at Baguashan, a detachment under Wu Pengnian marched north to help.
codex.fm_blackflag.design: The strongest unit on the Taiwanese side, with range equal to Japanese infantry.
codex.fm_militia.title: Militia
codex.fm_militia.intro: Armed groups formed spontaneously across Taiwan; Hakka militias were especially active.
codex.fm_militia.history: Wu Tangxing, Jiang Shaozu, Xu Xiang and others raised local volunteers around Taoyuan, Hsinchu and Miaoli, armed with everything from modern rifles to old firearms; women also fought and carried supplies.
codex.fm_militia.design: Hidden in hills, mountains and forests; knows the terrain and moves fast. Good for ambushing supply carts with hit-and-run attacks.
codex.fm_fort.title: Battery
codex.fm_fort.intro: Coastal defense and fortress batteries left from the Qing era.
codex.fm_fort.history: The Shiqiuling Battery guarded the road from Keelung to Taipei; on Baguashan about four hundred men manned 17 cm Krupp breech-loaders, shelling the Japanese across the Dadu River.
codex.fm_fort.design: Range 11 (+1 on high ground); crossfire bonus when two or more cover the same target.
codex.liu_yongfu.title: Liu Yongfu
codex.liu_yongfu.intro: Leader of the Black Flag Army and second president of the Republic of Formosa.
codex.liu_yongfu.history: Stationed in Tainan in 1895. After Tang Jingsong fled, he succeeded him as president on 26 June. In October he offered the Japanese a conditional surrender, which was refused, and on the 20th he left by ship for the mainland in disguise.
codex.liu_yongfu.design: Hero: nearby units +15% attack. In chapter 4 you can choose to leave for the mainland to end the chapter (the historical outcome); if he is killed, the result is worse than in history.
codex.wu_tangxing.title: Wu Tangxing
codex.wu_tangxing.intro: Hakka from Miaoli, commander of Taiwan's militias.
codex.wu_tangxing.history: He raised militias against the Japanese around Taoyuan, Hsinchu and Miaoli, then led them south to join the Black Flag Army in defending Baguashan, where he was killed.
codex.wu_tangxing.design: Hero: nearby militia +10% attack; can hide in hills and forests.
codex.jiang_shaozu.title: Jiang Shaozu
codex.jiang_shaozu.intro: Hakka gentleman from Beipu, Hsinchu, and militia leader.
codex.jiang_shaozu.history: He spent his family fortune to raise a militia and fought around Hsinchu; captured, he took poison at only twenty-one.
codex.xu_xiang.title: Xu Xiang
codex.xu_xiang.history: He fought across Taoyuan–Hsinchu–Miaoli, Baguashan and Chiayi, and was finally killed near Tainan.
codex.wu_pengnian.title: Wu Pengnian
codex.wu_pengnian.intro: Aide to Liu Yongfu and a Black Flag Army commander.
codex.wu_pengnian.history: Led the Black Flag Army north to reinforce Changhua and was killed in the Battle of Baguashan.
codex.kitashirakawa.title: Prince Kitashirakawa Yoshihisa
codex.kitashirakawa.intro: Member of the Japanese imperial family; commander of the Imperial Guard Division.
codex.kitashirakawa.history: Landed at Aodi with the Imperial Guard Division and pushed south; died in Tainan on 28 October.
codex.kitashirakawa.dispute: Disputed: some sources say he died of malaria, others of wounds; some researchers regard the story that he was "wounded at Baguashan" as folklore.
codex.nogi.title: Nogi Maresuke
codex.nogi.history: In October 1895 he landed at Fangliao with the 2nd Division and advanced north to encircle Tainan; from 1896 he served as the third Governor-General of Taiwan.
codex.nogi.design: Hero: nearby units +15% attack. Commander of the southern column in Chapter 4.
codex.y_tang.title: Tang Jingsong and Qiu Fengjia
codex.y_tang.intro: President and vice president of the Republic of Formosa.
codex.y_tang.history: Tang Jingsong, formerly Governor of Taiwan, was chosen as president; after Keelung fell he fled to Xiamen in disguise on 6 June. Qiu Fengjia, vice president and militia commissioner, led the founding of the Republic and later also left for the mainland.
codex.y_tang.design: Neither appears on the battlefield; Tang Jingsong's flight in Chapter 1 is shown as a scripted event.
codex.y_keelung.title: Keelung and Shiqiuling
codex.y_keelung.history: From Aodi the Japanese army crossed Sandiaoling and took Keelung by way of Ruifang; the Shiqiuling fort guarded the road from Keelung to Taipei.
codex.y_keelung.design: In Chapter 1 the Japanese army must destroy the Shiqiuling fort and secure Keelung.
codex.y_baguashan.title: Baguashan
codex.y_baguashan.intro: A plateau east of Changhua city.
codex.y_baguashan.history: Site of the largest pitched battle of the 1895 war.
codex.y_baguashan.design: Chapter 3: the battle opens at night (reduced vision), and units wading the Dadu River take 30% more damage.
codex.y_baguashan.dispute: Disputed: Chinese accounts say the fighting ended on the morning of 28 August; most English accounts give 27 August.
codex.y_republic.title: What Was the Republic of Formosa?
codex.y_republic.intro: What it was is still debated.
codex.y_republic.history: Founded on 23 or 25 May 1895 (accounts differ), with a yellow tiger on a blue field as its flag and the era name "Yongqing". Some see it as one of Asia's first republics; others as a stopgap by officials and gentry to delay the cession and await foreign intervention; still others stress that it continued to profess loyalty to the Qing.
codex.y_republic.design: This game does not pass judgment; it presents the participants through their own motives and actions.
codex.y_republic.dispute: Disputed: the Republic's nature, the extent of popular support and its founding date are all contested.
codex.y_numbers.title: Forces and Casualties, 1895
codex.y_numbers.history: The Japanese force numbered 49,866 officers and men plus 26,787 laborers. Japanese killed in action: 164 or 333 (accounts differ); deaths from disease: 4,642 or 6,903. Japanese medical records give 8,503 deaths in total, including cholera 3,916, beriberi 1,275, dysentery 715 and malaria 668. Estimates of Taiwanese dead range from about 1,500 (regular troops), to 7,000–8,000, to at least 14,000 (including civilians).
codex.y_numbers.design: The game scales forces at roughly 1:150.
codex.y_numbers.dispute: Disputed: force and casualty figures vary by source, and civilian casualties are especially hard to estimate.
codex.y_reprisals.title: What Civilians Suffered
codex.y_reprisals.intro: Village burnings and massacres of civilians during the war.
codex.y_reprisals.history: From late July the Japanese army carried out sweeps that burned villages between Taipei and Hsinchu; on 20 October villagers around Soulang (Xiaolong) were killed (recorded as over 2,000). Other accounts record looting by routed Qing soldiers and local armed groups before and after the fighting. Estimates of civilian casualties vary enormously.
codex.y_reprisals.design: This game does not depict atrocities against civilians on screen; they are covered only in text on history cards and in the Codex.
codex.y_reprisals.dispute: Disputed: the scale and death tolls of each incident differ greatly between Japanese records, Taiwanese accounts and later research.

history.penghu3: Tungning · History: After the defeat at Penghu, the Tungning court split in two. Secretariat drafter Zheng Dexiao, Jianwei commander Huang Liangji, naval commander Xiao Wu, Central Command officer Hong Gongzhu and others urged an expedition to Luzon to continue the Ming Zheng regime; Liu Guoxuan argued for negotiation. Feng Xifan first leaned toward fighting on but then followed Liu Guoxuan and chose surrender. On the 15th day of the 7th month (lunar calendar) Zheng Keshuang was placed in Shi Lang's hands; on the 3rd day of the 10th month Shi Lang entered Taiwan to accept the surrender, and on the 8th Zheng Keshuang and his civil and military officials shaved their heads and submitted to the Qing. The Zheng family was sent to Beijing and enrolled in the Han Chinese Plain Yellow Banner. The following year the Qing court debated whether to abandon Taiwan; Shi Lang submitted his "Memorial on Keeping or Abandoning Taiwan" urging that it be kept, and the Qing established Taiwan Prefecture under Fujian Province.
cut.penghu3_intro.title: Tungning · Summer 1683
cut.penghu3_intro.1: Liu Guoxuan escapes back to Taiwan through Houmen with news that the whole army at Penghu has been destroyed. In the court at Chengtian Prefecture, the fourteen-year-old Prince of Yanping, Zheng Keshuang, sits on the throne, but real power lies with Feng Xifan and Liu Guoxuan.
cut.penghu3_intro.2: Some urge sailing south to Luzon to build anew; others believe the cause is lost and that they should protect the people and surrender to the Qing.
cut.penghu3_intro.3: Shi Lang's fleet has already appeared off Taijiang. Tungning must decide.

history.yiwei5: Truku · History: After 1895 Japanese rule was established in the lowlands, but the indigenous peoples of the mountains resisted for nearly twenty more years. The Government-General encircled the mountains with the "aiyong" guardline and cut off salt and iron; clashes such as the 1896 Xincheng Incident and the 1906 Weili Incident followed. From 1910 the fifth Governor-General, Sakuma Samata, pursued the "Five-Year Riban Plan" (for controlling the aborigines). From 17 May to 28 August 1914, Sakuma personally directed the army, police columns and large numbers of porters in a two-pronged attack on the Truku from east and west, the largest war on the island of Taiwan in the twentieth century. Kbayang fell on 14 June; on the 26th Sakuma was injured in a fall from a cliff (he died the next year); on 3 July paramount chief Haruq Nawi led his people in surrendering their arms. Japanese casualties were about 364; Truku casualties were not recorded. After the war their guns were confiscated and the people were relocated en masse to the lowlands. In 1930 the Seediq rose up at Musha.
cut.yiwei5_intro.title: Truku · 1914
cut.yiwei5_intro.1: After the 1895 war, resistance in the lowlands was gradually suppressed, but in the Central Mountain Range the indigenous peoples had not submitted. The Government-General built a guardline along the foothills, cutting off salt, iron and ammunition.
cut.yiwei5_intro.2: In 1910 Governor-General Sakuma Samata, the same officer who had led the cliff assault at Stone Gate forty years earlier, launched the "Five-Year Riban Plan". One mountain region after another was encircled and taken.
cut.yiwei5_intro.3: The last to remain were the Truku of the Liwu River valley. They had several thousand men able to fight, who knew every cliff and hunting trail.
cut.yiwei5_intro.4: In May 1914 the Japanese entered Truku by two routes: the army from Mount Hehuan and the police from Xincheng in Hualien.
codex.e_tungning_court.title: Tungning's Last Council
codex.e_tungning_court.intro: Surrender to the Qing, sail to Luzon, or hold to the end?
codex.e_tungning_court.history: The war party (Zheng Dexiao, Huang Liangji, Xiao Wu, Hong Gongzhu and others) urged an expedition to Luzon; Liu Guoxuan favored peace; Feng Xifan first leaned toward fighting, then followed Liu Guoxuan, and surrender was decided.

codex.e_zheng_keshuang.title: Zheng Keshuang
codex.e_zheng_keshuang.intro: The last Ming Zheng Prince of Yanping.
codex.e_zheng_keshuang.history: Son of Zheng Jing; he succeeded as a boy after the Tungning coup, with real power in Feng Xifan's hands. After surrendering, his family was moved to Beijing and enrolled in the Han Chinese Plain Yellow Banner, and he was made a duke of the Han Banners. In 1699 he had the remains of Koxinga and Zheng Jing returned to Quanzhou for burial; he died in Beijing in 1707.
codex.e_zheng_keshuang.design: Does not appear on the battlefield.
codex.haruq_nawi.title: Haruq Nawi
codex.haruq_nawi.history: Led Truku resistance to the Japanese offensive in 1914 and on 3 July led his people in surrendering their arms. His name is rendered differently across sources (often Holok Naowi in English).

codex.e_truku.title: Truku and the Liwu River
codex.e_truku.intro: The gorge country on the east side of the Central Mountain Range.
codex.e_truku.history: Truku villages lay on terraces along the Liwu River valley. After the war the Japanese administered the area through the Xincheng and Inner Truku sub-prefectures.
codex.e_truku.design: The map is schematic: the Japanese western column descends from Mount Hehuan, and the eastern column climbs the Liwu River from Xincheng.
codex.e_riban.title: The Guardline and the Five-Year Riban Plan
codex.e_riban.intro: The Government-General's military and blockade policy toward the mountain peoples.
codex.e_riban.history: The Government-General built guardlines along the mountains (some electrified or mined) and pushed them steadily into the highlands. The "Five-Year Riban Plan" of 1910–1915 used force to make each people surrender their arms and submit; the Truku War was its largest campaign.
codex.e_riban.design: The guardline posts at both ends of the map fire on approaching Truku warriors.
codex.e_riban.dispute: Disputed: "Riban" (aboriginal control) was the official term of the time, used in this game only when naming the policy. Japanese records and indigenous oral accounts often differ on the course and casualties of each clash.
codex.e_truku_numbers.title: Forces and Casualties, 1914
codex.e_truku_numbers.intro: Japanese figures are complete; Truku figures are almost unrecorded.
codex.e_truku_numbers.history: The Japanese force numbered about 11,000 (some say about 20,000), plus about 400 Seediq "mikata-ban" (allied indigenous fighters) and many porters. The Truku had about 2,350–3,000 fighting men (some say about 5,000). Japanese casualties were about 364 (police 138, army 226); Truku casualties were not recorded.
codex.e_truku_numbers.design: The game scales forces at roughly 1:200.
codex.e_truku_numbers.dispute: Disputed: estimates of both sides' strength vary widely, and Truku losses can only be estimated from oral accounts and scattered records.

history.wushe1: The Uprising · History: At dawn on 27 October 1930, Mona Rudo, chief of Mahebu, led the six Tgdaya villages (Mahebu, Gungu, Truwan, Boarung, Suku and Drodux) in an uprising. They attacked the Mahebu, Boarung, Sakura, Gungu, Tunbara, Onoe, Nōkō and other police posts, seizing 180 rifles and 23,037 rounds. At about 8 a.m. they attacked the Musha Public School, where a joint sports day was under way, along with the police branch office, post office and staff quarters. 134 Japanese were killed (including women and children) and 215 wounded; two Han Taiwanese wearing kimono were also killed by mistake. This game does not depict the killing at the sports day. The Japanese relief force was held up by sniper fire on the 28th, and army troops entered Musha on the 29th. Causes of the uprising included forced labor and unfair wages, abuse by police, bans on traditional tattooing and hunting, and the "wine-toast incident" of 7 October.
cut.wushe1_intro.title: Musha · October 1930
cut.wushe1_intro.1: Sixteen years have passed since the Truku War. The Japanese call Musha a model district of "Riban" (aboriginal control), with a school, post office, inn and shops; but the Seediq are forced to haul timber and build quarters, and their wages are often withheld.
cut.wushe1_intro.2: On 7 October, at a wedding feast, a young man from Mahebu offered a toast to police officer Yoshimura Katsumi. Yoshimura complained that his hands were dirty and struck him with a cane. Chief Mona Rudo brought his son to apologize, but the matter did not die down.
cut.wushe1_intro.3: Mona Rudo and the chiefs of the other villages secretly agreed to rise on the 27th, during the Musha sports day, when Japanese officials and police would all be gathered in Musha.
cut.wushe1_intro.4: At dawn on the 27th, warriors of the six villages split up to strike the police posts.
