history.wushe2: Mahebu · History: The Japanese mobilized about 1,194 soldiers and about 1,306 police, plus about 450 "mikata-ban" (allied indigenous fighters) from the Toda, Truku (the Seediq Truku group), Vanda, Hakaw, Paran and other groups, along with aircraft and mountain guns. The offensive began on 31 October; on 1 November the Truwan line fell under bombing and Tadao Nokan was killed; Mahebu was taken on the 2nd. On the 5th there was heavy fighting near the Mahebu cave, and Mona Rudo's second son, Basaw Mona, was badly wounded. The Japanese then besieged the cave with mountain guns, aerial bombs and poison gas (the type of gas is disputed). Mona Rudo took his own life in the mountains in late November; his eldest son, Tado Mona, hanged himself on 8 December, and many Seediq died in mass suicides by hanging. About 644 Seediq died, 296 of them by hanging; about 28 Japanese soldiers and police died, and 22 mikata-ban. On 25 April 1931 the Toda attacked surrendered Seediq held in detention camps, killing 216 (the Second Musha Incident); the 298 survivors were moved to Kawanakajima (today Qingliu).
cut.wushe2_intro.title: Mahebu · November 1930
cut.wushe2_intro.1: The Japanese bring in troops and police from Taipei, Taichung, Tainan and Hualien Harbor, and the air unit from Pingtung flies over Musha. The Toda and other groups with old grievances against the six villages are mobilized as well.
cut.wushe2_intro.2: The Seediq abandon Musha and fall back up the Zhuoshui River, holding two lines at Truwan and Mahebu. Their last refuge is the cave in the cliffs behind Mahebu.
cut.wushe2_intro.3: The captured rounds are few. Every shot must count.
codex.mona_rudao.title: Mona Rudo
codex.mona_rudao.intro: Chief of Mahebu and leader of the Musha Incident.
codex.mona_rudao.history: In his youth he resisted Japanese rule several times and was also taken on a tour of Japan. In 1930 he led the six villages in the uprising; in late November he took his own life in the mountains (his wife hanged herself first; he shot two grandsons and then himself). His remains were found in 1934, put on public display and sent to Taipei; they were reburied at Musha in 1973.
codex.mona_rudao.design: Hero: nearby warriors +10% attack; can hide in mountain forest. His death is told only in text; his suicide is not shown.
codex.tado_nokan.title: Tadao Nokan
codex.tado_nokan.history: Killed on 1 November 1930 under Japanese bombing and assault; the Truwan line was lost.
codex.tado_nokan.design: A melee hero who appears at Truwan in Chapter 2.
codex.tado_nokan.dispute: Disputed: the same Chinese Wikipedia article calls him chief of Truwan in one place and of Gungu in another.
codex.w_hanaoka.title: Hanaoka Ichirō and Hanaoka Jirō
codex.w_hanaoka.history: Two young Seediq men whom the Japanese held up as products of "Riban" (aboriginal control), serving as police officers. During the incident both took their own lives along with their families, Ichirō by seppuku.
codex.w_hanaoka.design: Do not appear on the battlefield.
codex.w_hanaoka.dispute: Disputed: whether the two helped plan the uprising, and what role they played that day, remains unresolved.
codex.w_seediq.title: The Tgdaya and Musha
codex.w_seediq.intro: The Seediq of the upper Zhuoshui River.
codex.w_seediq.history: The Tgdaya had more than ten villages. The six that rose up were Mahebu, Gungu, Truwan, Boarung, Suku and Drodux, with 1,236 people taking part. Paran, the most populous village, did not join because its chief, Walis Buni, opposed the uprising. Musha lies in today's Ren'ai Township, Nantou County.
codex.w_seediq.design: The map is schematic: in the west is the Meixi mountain road toward Puli, in the center the Musha plateau, and to the east, up the Zhuoshui River, the villages and Mahebu.
codex.w_cave.title: Mahebu Cave
codex.w_cave.history: A cave in the cliffs behind Mahebu. On 5 November about two hours of heavy fighting on the nearby heights cost the Japanese Tainan unit 15 dead and 13 wounded; the Japanese then besieged it with mountain guns, aerial bombs and gas shells.
codex.w_cave.design: The final objective of Chapter 2: the Japanese must reduce the Seediq on the cave heights to fewer than 3 and hold for 30 seconds.
codex.w_causes.title: Causes of the Uprising
codex.w_causes.intro: Forced labor, abuse and the wine-toast incident.
codex.w_causes.history: The Seediq were forced to haul timber and build quarters and schools, and their wages were often withheld; police officers marrying Seediq women and then abandoning them was a common story; traditional tattooing and hunting were restricted. On 7 October 1930 police officer Yoshimura Katsumi struck a young man who offered him a toast at a wedding feast (the "wine-toast incident"), and this became the spark.
codex.w_causes.design: Chapter 1's cutscene opens with these causes.
codex.w_school.title: The Musha Public School Sports Day
codex.w_school.intro: What happened on the morning of 27 October.
codex.w_school.history: At about 8 a.m. that day, the Seediq attacked the Musha Public School during a joint sports day. 134 Japanese were killed (including women and children), and two Han Taiwanese wearing kimono were also killed by mistake.
codex.w_school.design: The school appears only as a landmark; it cannot be attacked and takes no part in combat. What happened at the sports day is told only in text and not shown on screen.
codex.w_gas.title: Air Raids and Poison Gas
codex.w_gas.history: The Japanese sent the Pingtung air unit to bomb and shelled with mountain guns; later tallies record 137 Seediq killed by bombing and 34 by shelling. The Japanese also used poison gas: on 3 November troops requested "corrosive" shells, and the reply on the 5th instructed that the gas be referred to by a code name.
codex.w_gas.design: Chapter 2's air raids are a game mechanic: red circles appear on the ground and bombs fall a few seconds later; forest or mountains reduce the damage. Poison gas is covered only here, in text.
codex.w_gas.dispute: Disputed: official records mention only tear gas; survivors described severe skin burns and deaths inside huts; Chinese Wikipedia describes a blister agent of the lewisite type, plus white phosphorus incendiaries; some research suggests a mixture of tear gas and cyanide of uncertain effect. Most scholars agree that poison gas was used.
codex.w_allies.title: Groups Allied with the Japanese (mikata-ban)
codex.w_allies.history: The Japanese mobilized about 450 fighters from the Toda, Truku (the Seediq Truku group), Vanda, Malepa, Hakaw, Paran and other groups, known at the time as "mikata-ban" (allied indigenous fighters). They had tangled histories with the six villages over hunting grounds and old grievances, and were also under Japanese pressure and offered bounties. On 11 November a party at Tunbara was ambushed and about 25, including a chief, were killed.
codex.w_allies.design: In Chapter 2, "Toda Fighters" are a Japanese-side unit. The term "mikata-ban" is used only when quoting the name of the time.
codex.w_allies.dispute: Disputed: Japanese records and indigenous oral accounts often differ on why each group joined (coercion, bounties or old grievances).
codex.w_aftermath.title: The Second Musha Incident and Kawanakajima
codex.w_aftermath.history: On 25 April 1931 the Toda attacked surrendered Seediq held in detention camps, killing 216 (other figures: 214 or 218). Japanese police knew in advance, and police officer Kojima Genji admitted in the 1970s that he had incited it. On 6 May the 298 survivors were forcibly moved to Kawanakajima (today Qingliu), and the six villages were merged. Governor-General Ishizuka Eizō and Chief Civil Administrator Hitomi Jirō left office over the incident.
codex.w_aftermath.design: Covered only in text on history cards and in the Codex.
codex.w_aftermath.dispute: Disputed: death tolls vary; the role of Japanese police in the second incident was admitted by those involved only after the war.
codex.w_numbers.title: Forces and Casualties
codex.w_numbers.history: 1,236 Seediq took part, about 300 of them able to fight. The Japanese had about 1,194 soldiers and about 1,306 police, plus about 450 mikata-ban. 134 Japanese civilians were killed; 22 soldiers, 6 police and 22 mikata-ban died. About 644 Seediq died: 85 by blade or gun, 137 by bombing, 34 by shelling, 87 beheaded by mikata-ban, and 296 by hanging; another 265 were captured and about 500 surrendered.
codex.w_numbers.design: The game scales the number of warriors at roughly 1:10, and Japanese forces by more.
codex.w_numbers.dispute: Disputed: most figures come from Japanese tallies after the fact; English Wikipedia gives about 2,000 Japanese, and Seediq oral accounts also differ from the Japanese figures.

hint.title: New mechanic
hint.wind: Wind: the vane at top right shows where the wind is blowing from. Sailing ships are up to 45% faster with the wind and up to 45% slower against it, and the wind shifts during battle.
hint.stealth: Forest stealth: warriors who know the mountain paths can only be seen by enemies within 1.5 tiles while in forest, hills or mountains; firing a matchlock or rifle briefly gives away their position with smoke.
hint.uphill: High ground: shooting downhill has the advantage; shooting uphill deals less damage.
hint.occupy: Occupying: you need the required number of units in the target area, with no enemy units there (or fewer than the stated number), for a set time. The defender only has to keep units in the area to stop the timer.
hint.supply: Supply lines: Japanese troops too far from a depot or supply wagon slowly lose morale, faster the farther they are. This alone won't make them break, but they fight worse. Cutting off the supply wagons is a key tactic for the Taiwanese side.
hint.night: Night battle: everyone's vision is reduced until dawn, and units wading across rivers take more damage.
hint.disease: Disease: the Japanese army steadily loses men to disease; the longer it drags on, the worse for them.
hint.rearm: Captured guns: when the Seediq take a police post or the Musha police branch office, nearby blade warriors switch to captured rifles and rounds (top left) increase. Riflemen out of rounds can only fight in melee.
hint.ammo: Limited rounds: each shot by a Seediq rifleman uses one round (top left); when they run out, only melee is possible. Guns and rounds captured in Chapter 1 carry over to this chapter.
hint.raid: Air raids: when red circles appear on the ground, bombs fall a few seconds later. Move units out of the circles, or take cover in forest or mountains to greatly reduce damage. The more crowded the units, the less damage each takes, but all of them are hit.
save.mismatch.title: This save is from an older version
save.mismatch.text: The game has been updated since this save (balance or AI behaviour may have changed). Loading normally replays your orders, but the AI re-decides under the new rules, so the battle may not match your save; restoring the snapshot returns to the latest checkpoint before the save (up to a minute earlier) with the state exactly as it was.

sf1.obj.hold: Hold the heights by Fort San Domingo for 12 minutes, or cut the landing force below 8 men
sf1.msg.bombard: The French ships open fire on the Tamsui forts.
sf1.msg.land: French sailors land near the New Fort!
sf1.msg.reserve: Zhang Gaoyuan's reserve arrives from the east.
sf1.msg.rounds: The French sailors are running out of rounds.
sf1.end.history: The landing force was checked among the hedges and re-embarked. As in history.
sf1.end.held: The French could not take the heights and re-embarked. As in history.
sf1.end.rout: The landing force was all but wiped out. Worse than in history.
sf1.end.taken: The French took the heights by Fort San Domingo and opened the Tamsui river (did not happen in history).
history.sf1: Tamsui – History: after a failed bombardment of Keelung in August 1884, Courbet took Keelung on 1 October and sent Lespès against Tamsui. The Qing had sunk stone-filled boats and laid nine mines in the river mouth, so the French ships could not enter. On 2 October they fired more than 2,000 shells and silenced the New Fort's guns. On 8 October about 600 sailors in five companies landed near the New Fort, lost their way among the dunes, hedges and scrub, and were ambushed by the troops of Sun Kaihua, Zhang Gaoyuan and Liu Chaoyou and by Tio Li-xieng's local braves. By noon they had used about two-thirds of their rounds; both flanks gave way, and a launch capsized during the re-embarkation. The French lost 17 dead and 49 wounded, the Qing about 80 dead and 200 wounded (according to European customs staff at Tamsui; Liu Mingchuan reported about 300 French dead, a figure considered inflated). French bodies left on the field and captured wounded were beheaded and displayed. The victory strengthened the war party at court, and the Guangxu Emperor credited it to the goddess Mazu. From 23 October the French blockaded Taiwan.
cut.sf1_intro.title: Tamsui, October 1884
cut.sf1_intro.1: France went to war with the Qing over Vietnam. In August its squadron sank the Fujian fleet at Mawei, then came to northern Taiwan to seize the Keelung coal mines as a bargaining chip.
cut.sf1_intro.2: Liu Mingchuan, in charge of Taiwan's defence, gave up Keelung and gathered his troops at Tamsui, the mouth of the river leading to Taipei.
cut.sf1_intro.3: The river mouth is blocked with sunken boats and mines. Sun Kaihua's troops and the local braves raised by Tio Li-xieng wait among the hedges and scrub behind the dunes.
cut.sf1_intro.4: At dawn on 2 October the French guns turn on the forts of Tamsui.
scenario.sf2.name: Yuemeishan
sf2.obj.take: Within 15 minutes take Hongdanshan and Yuemeishan (5 men, fewer than 2 Qing, 45 s each); disease thins the ranks and rain spoils aim
sf2.obj.hold: Hold the ridge for 15 minutes, or cut the French below 8; if the ridge falls, hold Nuannuan south of the Keelung River
sf2.msg.rain: Torrential rain: shots go wide and sight shrinks.
sf2.msg.flank: French reinforcements swing round by the east coast against the flank of Yuemeishan!
sf2.msg.heights: The ridge is lost; the Qing fall back across the Keelung River.
sf2.msg.lin: Lin Chaodong is wounded and withdraws.
sf2.end.history: The French took Yuemeishan; the Qing held the south bank of the Keelung River, and the two sides were deadlocked. As in history.
sf2.end.crushed: The French took Nuannuan too, opening the road to Taipei. Worse than in history.
sf2.end.repulsed: French losses and sickness halted the offensive (did not happen in history).
sf2.end.held: The French could not take the ridge within 15 minutes (did not happen in history).
history.sf2: Yuemeishan – History: after taking Keelung the French were penned in around the harbour; from November cholera and typhus spread, and by early December only about 1,100 men were fit to fight. Reinforcements in January 1885 brought them to about 4,000. In the first battle of Yuemeishan (25–31 January) they took the forward heights but stopped on the 28th in heavy rain, losing 21 dead and 62 wounded; Qing losses were put at no fewer than 2,000, among them the battalion commander Zhang Rengui. On 4–7 March about 1,300 French troops turned the line from the east and took Yuemeishan and Hongdanshan after hard fighting on the Niaozui ridge, losing 41 dead and 157 wounded against about 1,500 Qing killed and wounded. On the 9th the Qing left Shiqiuling and fell back to Nuannuan on the south bank of the Keelung River; the French stopped on the north bank. The defenders were led by Cao Zhizhong and Lin Chaodong (with the Wufeng Lin family's Dong Army). In the whole Keelung campaign the French lost 600–700 dead, most of them to disease.
cut.sf2_intro.title: Keelung, early 1885
cut.sf2_intro.1: The French have held Keelung for three months but cannot break out of the hills around the harbour. Cholera and typhus fill the camp with more sick than fit.
cut.sf2_intro.2: The Qing have dug trenches along the ridge from Hongdanshan over Niaozui to Yuemeishan; Lin Chaodong of the Wufeng Lin family holds the eastern end with his Dong Army.
cut.sf2_intro.3: Reinforcements have arrived. Lieutenant-Colonel Duchesne decides to storm the ridge.
scenario.sf3.name: Penghu
sf3.obj.take: Bombard, land, and within 12 minutes take Makung (6 men, fewer than 2 Qing, held 60 s)
sf3.obj.hold: Hold Makung for 12 minutes, or cut the landing force below 5 men
sf3.msg.land: French marines land south-east of Makung!
sf3.msg.courbet: The Bayard is sunk (historically Courbet died of illness aboard the Bayard in Makung harbour in June).
sf3.end.history: The French took Makung and held Penghu until they withdrew after the peace. As in history.
sf3.end.repulsed: The landing was thrown back and the French gave up on Penghu (did not happen in history).
sf3.end.held: The French could not take Makung within 12 minutes (did not happen in history).
history.sf3: Penghu – History: with Keelung deadlocked, Courbet turned on Penghu to gain a base for blockading the Taiwan Strait. On 29 March his six warships shelled Makung and the surrounding batteries; that evening about 400 marines with two mountain guns landed, broke the chain barrier across the bay on the 30th, and occupied Makung on the 31st. The roughly 2,400 defenders under Zhou Shanchu and Zheng Yingjie lost about 300 dead and 400–500 wounded; the French lost 5 dead and 12 wounded. A ceasefire followed on 4 April, and the Sino-French treaty was signed at Tianjin on 9 June. On 11 June Courbet died of illness aboard the Bayard in Makung harbour. The French left Keelung on 22 June and Penghu on 22 July. After the war the Qing paid new attention to Taiwan's defence: Taiwan became a province, with Liu Mingchuan leading its reforms.
cut.sf3_intro.title: Penghu, March 1885
cut.sf3_intro.1: On the hills of Keelung neither side can move the other. Courbet looks to Penghu: hold Makung harbour, and he can close the whole Taiwan Strait.
cut.sf3_intro.2: Two hundred years ago Shi Lang destroyed the Tungning fleet here. Now Makung's batteries carry Armstrong guns, and a chain closes the bay.
cut.sf3_intro.3: On 29 March steam warships that wait for no wind sail into Penghu.
hint.sailor_rounds: Limited rounds: each shot by the French sailors uses one round (top left); out of rounds, they can only fight hand to hand. Naval gunfire can soften the defenders first.
hint.hedges: Ambush in the hedges: village militia and local braves in hedges and scrub (forest tiles) cannot be seen until the enemy is within 2 tiles.
hint.navalfire: Naval gunfire: when a red ring appears, the warships' shells land a few seconds later. Move out of the ring, or take cover in forest or on mountains; the shelling goes on while French ships remain.
hint.disease_fr: Disease: cholera and typhus keep thinning the French ranks; the longer it lasts, the worse for the French.
hint.rain: Rain: while it rains, everyone's shots miss more often and sight shrinks.
hint.steam: Steam warships: the French ships of 1885 ignore the wind and outrange the old shore batteries.
codex.liu_mingchuan.title: Liu Mingchuan
codex.liu_mingchuan.intro: The Huai Army general in charge of Taiwan's defence.
codex.liu_mingchuan.history: Sent in 1884 to run Taiwan's defence, he gave up Keelung to save Tamsui, then held the French along the Keelung River. After the war Taiwan became a province, and he pushed railways, telegraphs and land surveys.
codex.liu_mingchuan.design: Hero: nearby troops +10% attack. In chapter 2 he holds Nuannuan.
codex.sun_kaihua.title: Sun Kaihua
codex.sun_kaihua.intro: Commander of the defence at Tamsui.
codex.sun_kaihua.history: A Xiang Army officer who built the New Fort at Tamsui in 1876; on 8 October 1884 he ambushed the French landing among the hedges.
codex.sun_kaihua.design: A melee hero who leads the charge.
codex.lin_chaodong.title: Lin Chaodong
codex.lin_chaodong.intro: Head of the Wufeng Lin family and commander of the Dong Army.
codex.lin_chaodong.history: He led the Dong Army, raised by his family, north to defend Keelung and fought at Yuemeishan. After the war he worked with Liu Mingchuan on opening the mountains and the camphor trade.
codex.lin_chaodong.design: Hero: fast in the mountains and hidden in the woods.
codex.courbet.title: Amédée Courbet
codex.courbet.intro: Commander of the French Far East Squadron.
codex.courbet.history: He sank the Fujian fleet at Mawei in August 1884, took Keelung in October and Penghu in March 1885, and died of illness aboard his flagship Bayard in Makung harbour on 11 June.
codex.sf_locals.title: Village militia, the Dong Army and local braves
codex.sf_locals.history: From October 1884 local militia joined the defence; the Wufeng Lin family's Dong Army came north to Keelung; at Tamsui, Tio Li-xieng led a battalion of local braves on the flank. The Chinese Wikipedia counts some 20,000 local braves across Taiwan.
codex.sf_locals.design: Militia and local braves hide in hedges and scrub, and the braves move fast; the Dong Army knows the mountains.
codex.sf_fleet.title: The French Far East Squadron
codex.sf_fleet.intro: The age of the steam ironclad.
codex.sf_fleet.history: Courbet's squadron had the ironclads Bayard, Triomphante and La Galissonnière, with cruisers and gunboats; at Tamsui the ships could not enter the river and fired from the sea.
codex.sf_fleet.design: Unaffected by the wind; range 10–11, beyond the shore batteries.
codex.sf_tamsui.title: Tamsui and Fort San Domingo
codex.sf_tamsui.intro: The mouth of the Tamsui river.
codex.sf_tamsui.history: Fort San Domingo was then the British consulate, with a Krupp battery on its hill; the New Fort and the White Fort guarded the river mouth. Fuyou Temple in Tamsui still commemorates the battle.
codex.sf_tamsui.design: Fort San Domingo is a landmark that cannot be attacked. The map is schematic.
codex.sf_keelung.title: The hills of Keelung
codex.sf_keelung.history: The French called Shiqiuling "La Dent", Hongdanshan "Le Cirque" and Yuemeishan "La Table".
codex.sf_keelung.design: The Qing trenches on the ridge give cover. The map is schematic.
codex.sf_war.title: Who won the Sino-French War?
codex.sf_war.history: France gained its protectorate over Vietnam but never broke out in Taiwan; the English Wikipedia infobox calls the Keelung campaign a Qing victory while its text describes a strategic and tactical stalemate. After Tamsui, French bodies left on the field and captured wounded were beheaded and displayed; the Guangxu Emperor credited the victory to Mazu.
codex.sf_war.design: Following the game's rules, the beheadings are told in text only, never shown.
codex.sf_war.dispute: Disputed: the two sides' accounts of casualties and outcome differ widely; Liu Mingchuan's reports are thought to inflate French losses.
codex.sf_aftermath.title: After the war: a province of Taiwan
codex.sf_aftermath.intro: The Qing take Taiwan's defence seriously.
codex.sf_aftermath.history: After the 1885 treaty the Qing separated Taiwan from Fujian as a province; Liu Mingchuan led railways, telegraphs, land surveys and the opening of the mountains.
codex.sf_aftermath.design: Told in the history cards and codex only.
codex.sf_numbers.title: Forces and losses
codex.sf_numbers.history: French: about 2,250 landed at Keelung, rising to about 4,000 by January 1885; about 600 sailors landed at Tamsui and about 400 men at Penghu. Qing: about 5,000 in northern Taiwan by late July 1884 and about 25,000 by year's end (another count: 16,000 soldiers and 20,000 local braves island-wide); about 1,000 at Tamsui (other estimates 2,000–4,000); about 2,400 on Penghu.
codex.sf_numbers.design: The game scales forces at roughly 1:20.
codex.sf_numbers.dispute: Disputed: French and Qing figures often differ widely, especially for the Tamsui garrison.
sf3.end.rout: Makung fell and its defenders were all but wiped out. Worse than in history.
timeline.title: Wars in Taiwan, 1661–1930
timeline.sub: Six campaigns and nineteen chapters in order of time. Pick one to go to its campaign and choose a side.
history.mudan1.losses: Real losses: about a dozen Paiwan dead (Aruqu and his son among them) and about a dozen Japanese killed; some 560 Japanese reportedly died of disease. (The game's armies are scaled down; for comparison only.)
history.penghu2.losses: Real losses (the whole Penghu battle): Shi Lang reported 329 Qing dead and 1,800 wounded; about 12,000 Zheng dead and over 190 ships lost. (The game's armies are scaled down; for comparison only.)
history.sf1.losses: Real losses: French 17 dead, 49 wounded; Qing about 80 dead, 200 wounded. (The game's armies are scaled down; for comparison only.)
history.sf2.losses: Real losses: in January, French 21 dead and 62 wounded, Qing at least 2,000; in March, French 41 dead and 157 wounded, Qing about 1,500 killed and wounded. In the whole Keelung campaign 600–700 French died, most of disease. (The game's armies are scaled down; for comparison only.)
history.sf3.losses: Real losses: French 5 dead, 12 wounded; Qing about 300 dead, 400–500 wounded. (The game's armies are scaled down; for comparison only.)
history.yiwei5.losses: Real losses: about 364 Japanese killed and wounded (138 police, 226 soldiers); Truku losses were never recorded. (The game's armies are scaled down; for comparison only.)
history.wushe1.losses: Real losses: on 27 October 134 Japanese died (women and children among them) and 215 were wounded, and two Han Taiwanese were killed by mistake; Seediq losses that day are unknown. (The game's armies are scaled down; for comparison only.)
history.wushe2.losses: Real losses: about 644 Seediq died (296 of them by suicide); 22 Japanese soldiers, 6 police and 22 allied indigenous fighters died. (The game's armies are scaled down; for comparison only.)
